title: The Complete Guide to the MRCP Part 1 Exam (2026)
excerpt: Everything you need to know about MRCP(UK) Part 1 in 2026: format, eligibility, scoring, fees, exam dates, the move to computer-based testing and the full specialty blueprint.
author: MedAscend Editorial Team
content:
## What is MRCP Part 1?

MRCP(UK) Part 1 is the first of three examinations leading to Membership of the Royal Colleges of Physicians of the United Kingdom. It is the entry point to Internal Medicine Training stage 2 and to higher specialty training in the UK, and it is widely recognised internationally as a benchmark of core medical knowledge. Part 1 tests the knowledge and understanding of the clinical sciences relevant to medical practice and of common or important disorders, to a level appropriate for a doctor entering specialist training.

## Exam format

Part 1 consists of two papers taken on the same day, each lasting three hours. Each paper contains 100 best-of-five questions, giving 200 questions in total. Every question presents a clinical scenario or a short statement followed by five options; you choose the single best answer. There is no negative marking, so an unanswered question is simply a lost mark and you should never leave a question blank.

The exam is entirely text-based. There are no images, ECG traces or radiographs in Part 1 (these appear in Part 2 Written). The questions therefore rely on interpretation of history, examination findings and numerical results such as blood tests, arterial blood gases and spirometry.

## Eligibility and attempts

You may sit Part 1 once you are at least 12 months past your primary medical qualification (graduation). Most UK trainees sit it during the second year of Foundation training or the first year of Internal Medicine Training, although timing is flexible. The Royal Colleges permit a maximum of six attempts at Part 1. Candidates who have exhausted their attempts must provide evidence of additional educational experience before being allowed a further sitting.

## Scoring and the pass mark

Raw marks are converted to a scaled score ranging from 200 to 800 using an equating process that adjusts for the difficulty of each diet. The pass mark is fixed at a scaled score of 540, which corresponds to roughly 60 percent of questions answered correctly, although the exact raw percentage varies slightly from diet to diet. Because scaling is criterion-referenced rather than norm-referenced, you are not competing against other candidates; you are being measured against a standard.

The overall pass rate for a diet is typically around 40 to 50 percent, and considerably higher for UK graduates sitting for the first time within two years of graduation. Results are released approximately six weeks after the exam date, and your feedback statement breaks down performance by specialty, which is invaluable for planning a resit if one is needed.

## Fees

For 2026 the examination fee is 489 pounds for candidates sitting in the UK and 655 pounds for international centres. Fees are payable at the time of application through the MRCP(UK) My MRCP(UK) portal, and applications open around three months before each diet and close roughly six weeks before the exam date. Late applications are not accepted.

## 2026 exam dates

| Diet | Exam date | Approximate results |
|---|---|---|
| 2026/1 | 28 January 2026 | Mid March 2026 |
| 2026/2 | 21 May 2026 | Early July 2026 |
| 2026/3 | 23 September 2026 | Early November 2026 |

Three diets a year means a failed attempt can be followed by a resit within four months, but the more important consequence is that you can choose a date that fits around rotations and annual leave.

## The move to computer-based testing

2026 marks the transition of Part 1 from paper-based delivery to computer-based testing at Pearson VUE or equivalent professional test centres. Candidates book a seat at a centre of their choice and complete the two papers on screen, with on-screen flagging, review and a countdown timer. The content and standard of the exam are unchanged, but the experience differs from paper: there is no physical answer sheet to transcribe onto, reading speed on screen may be slightly slower for some candidates, and the ability to return to flagged questions is built into the interface. Practising with an online question bank in timed mode is therefore closer to the real thing than ever before.

## The specialty blueprint

The composition of each diet is fixed by a blueprint that sets the number of questions per specialty across the 200 questions. Knowing this distribution is the single most useful piece of strategic information available to you.

| Specialty | Questions |
|---|---|
| Cardiology | 14 |
| Clinical Pharmacology & Therapeutics | 15 |
| Clinical Sciences | 25 |
| Dermatology | 8 |
| Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolic Medicine | 14 |
| Gastroenterology & Hepatology | 14 |
| Geriatric Medicine | 8 |
| Haematology | 10 |
| Infectious Diseases | 14 |
| Neurology | 14 |
| Oncology | 5 |
| Medical Ophthalmology | 4 |
| Palliative Medicine & End of Life Care | 4 |
| Psychiatry | 9 |
| Renal Medicine | 14 |
| Respiratory Medicine | 14 |
| Rheumatology | 14 |
| Total | 200 |

Clinical Sciences is the largest single block at 25 questions. It covers cell, molecular and membrane biology, clinical anatomy, clinical biochemistry and metabolism, clinical physiology, genetics, immunology and statistics, epidemiology and evidence-based medicine. Clinical Pharmacology at 15 questions is the next largest, and it rewards systematic learning of adverse effects, interactions and mechanisms. Together these two blocks account for a fifth of the exam and are areas where many clinically experienced candidates underperform because they are rarely revisited after medical school.

The eight specialties worth 14 questions each (Cardiology, Endocrinology, Gastroenterology, Infectious Diseases, Neurology, Renal, Respiratory and Rheumatology) form the core of the exam at 112 questions between them. The smaller specialties (Oncology, Medical Ophthalmology, Palliative Medicine) contribute only 13 questions combined and should be revised efficiently rather than exhaustively.

## How to use this information

Weight your revision time roughly in proportion to the blueprint, but adjust for your own strengths. A candidate from a cardiology-heavy rotation may need far less time on Cardiology and far more on Clinical Sciences. MedAscend's textbook topics and question bank are organised by these exact specialty headings so that you can map your progress directly onto the blueprint.

## Summary

Part 1 is a 200-question, six-hour, best-of-five knowledge test with no negative marking, a fixed scaled pass mark of 540 and a maximum of six attempts. In 2026 it moves to computer-based delivery with three diets in January, May and September. Learn the blueprint, build a plan around it, and start practising questions early.

title: A 12-Week MRCP Part 1 Revision Timetable That Actually Works
excerpt: A realistic, blueprint-weighted 12-week plan for busy junior doctors, with weekly targets, question volumes and built-in consolidation.
author: MedAscend Editorial Team
content:
## Why twelve weeks?

Most successful first-time candidates report between 10 and 16 weeks of focused preparation alongside full-time clinical work. Twelve weeks is long enough to cover the whole blueprint twice and complete 3,000 to 4,000 practice questions, yet short enough to sustain momentum and fit within a single rotation. This plan assumes roughly 12 to 15 hours of study per week: around 90 minutes on weekday evenings plus one longer weekend session. If you are on nights or a heavy on-call block, stretch the plan to 14 weeks rather than cramming.

## The principles behind the plan

- Weight your time by the specialty blueprint: Clinical Sciences (25 questions) and Clinical Pharmacology (15) get the most time, the eight 14-question specialties get a full week each or shared weeks, and the small specialties are grouped
- Questions from day one: reading without testing produces an illusion of competence. Every study session ends with questions on the topic just revised
- Two passes: the first pass builds understanding, the second consolidates and exposes what has not stuck
- Spaced review: each week includes a short mixed block of questions from all previous weeks
- Protected mocks: three full-length timed sittings in the final four weeks

## Phase 1: foundations (weeks 1-4)

**Week 1: Clinical Sciences part 1.** Statistics and evidence-based medicine, genetics, immunology. Learn the two-by-two table cold, the inheritance patterns and the immunodeficiency syndromes. Target: 250 questions.

**Week 2: Clinical Sciences part 2 and Clinical Pharmacology.** Cell biology, physiology, biochemistry, anatomy. Then pharmacokinetics, cytochrome P450 interactions, adverse effects by drug class and poisoning. Target: 300 questions.

**Week 3: Cardiology and Respiratory Medicine.** Acute coronary syndromes, arrhythmias, heart failure, valvular disease, cardiomyopathies and ECG interpretation from text descriptions; asthma, COPD, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary embolism, lung cancer, pleural disease and lung function tests. Target: 300 questions.

**Week 4: Endocrinology and Renal Medicine.** Thyroid, adrenal, pituitary, diabetes and its complications, calcium and bone metabolism; acute kidney injury, glomerulonephritis, electrolyte and acid-base disorders, chronic kidney disease. Target: 300 questions.

## Phase 2: core specialties (weeks 5-8)

**Week 5: Gastroenterology and Hepatology.** Inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, liver disease and cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, pancreatitis, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, nutrition. Target: 300 questions plus a 50-question mixed review.

**Week 6: Neurology.** Stroke, epilepsy, headache, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson disease and movement disorders, neuromuscular disease, neuropathy, localisation of lesions. Target: 300 questions plus mixed review.

**Week 7: Infectious Diseases and Haematology.** HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and travel infection, antimicrobials, sepsis, notifiable diseases; anaemia, haemolysis, haematological malignancy, coagulation, transfusion. Target: 300 questions plus mixed review.

**Week 8: Rheumatology, Dermatology and Medical Ophthalmology.** Rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthritis, connective tissue disease, vasculitis, gout; psoriasis, eczema, skin cancer, blistering disorders, cutaneous signs of systemic disease; the red eye, retinal vascular disease, uveitis. Target: 300 questions plus mixed review.

## Phase 3: small specialties and first mock (weeks 9-10)

**Week 9: Psychiatry, Geriatric Medicine, Oncology and Palliative Medicine.** Depression, psychosis, antidepressants and antipsychotics, eating disorders, alcohol; delirium, falls, dementia, frailty, prescribing in older adults; oncological emergencies, tumour markers, paraneoplastic syndromes; opioid conversions and end-of-life symptom control. Target: 250 questions. Then sit **Mock 1** at the weekend: 200 questions in two timed three-hour papers. Review every incorrect and every guessed question over the following two evenings.

**Week 10: Targeted repair.** Use the mock analytics to rank your specialties from weakest to strongest. Spend the week on the bottom four, re-reading the textbook topics and doing 100 questions in each. Target: 400 questions.

## Phase 4: consolidation (weeks 11-12)

**Week 11: Second pass, high-yield.** Work through all your flagged questions and saved notes. Do daily mixed timed blocks of 50 questions rotating through every specialty. Sit **Mock 2** at the weekend and review it thoroughly.

**Week 12: Final week.** Light, mixed-question days of 60 to 100 questions with rapid review. Re-read your one-page summaries of statistics formulae, opioid conversions, antibody associations, cytochrome P450 lists and inheritance patterns. Sit **Mock 3** no later than four days before the exam so that its lessons can be absorbed without inducing panic. The last two days should be short sessions, early nights and logistics: test centre location, identification documents, travel plan.

## Weekly rhythm

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | 90 minutes: read topic, 40 questions in tutor mode |
| Tuesday | 90 minutes: read topic, 40 questions in tutor mode |
| Wednesday | 60 minutes: 50 mixed questions from previous weeks, timed |
| Thursday | 90 minutes: read topic, 40 questions in tutor mode |
| Friday | Rest or 30 minutes of flashcards |
| Saturday | 3 hours: remaining topics, 100 questions timed, review |
| Sunday | 2 hours: review all incorrect answers from the week, update notes |

## Making it stick

Keep a single running document of facts you got wrong, organised by specialty. Rewriting a fact in your own words when you miss it is worth more than reading it three times. Use MedAscend's spaced-repetition flashcards for the highest-density material: statistics, pharmacology, genetics and antibody associations. Protect your sleep in the final fortnight; memory consolidation happens overnight and a tired brain misreads best-of-five stems.

Finally, be realistic and forgiving. Almost nobody follows a plan perfectly. If you fall behind, cut the reading and keep the questions. Answering and reviewing questions is the highest-yield activity you can do, and it should be the last thing to be sacrificed.

title: How to Use a Question Bank Effectively for MRCP Part 1
excerpt: Tutor mode, timed mode, spaced repetition and the art of reviewing wrong answers: a practical method for turning thousands of practice questions into a pass.
author: MedAscend Editorial Team
content:
## Questions are the curriculum

For a best-of-five exam like MRCP Part 1, a question bank is not a supplement to revision; it is the main event. Retrieval practice, the act of pulling information out of memory to answer a question, strengthens memory far more than re-reading, and questions expose exactly what the examiners consider important. Most successful candidates complete between 3,000 and 5,000 questions before the exam, but volume alone is not the point. Two candidates can do the same 4,000 questions and get very different results depending on how they use them.

## Tutor mode versus timed mode

Question banks typically offer two modes, and each has a distinct job.

**Tutor mode** shows the answer and explanation immediately after each question. Use it when you are learning a topic for the first time or returning to a weak area. The immediate feedback closes the loop while the reasoning is still in your working memory, which is when correction is most effective. Read the explanation in full even when you were right, because best-of-five explanations usually discuss why each distractor is wrong and that is where the extra marks live.

**Timed mode** presents a block of questions under exam conditions with the explanations withheld until the end. Use it to build stamina, calibrate your pace and rehearse the psychological reality of the exam: not knowing whether you are doing well. Aim for a pace of around 90 seconds per question, which leaves a buffer for review within each three-hour paper. From the midpoint of your revision, at least a third of your questions should be in timed mode, rising to most of them in the final fortnight.

| | Tutor mode | Timed mode |
|---|---|---|
| Best for | Learning, weak specialties | Consolidation, exam rehearsal |
| Feedback | Immediate | After the block |
| Block size | 20-40 questions | 50-100 questions |
| When | Weeks 1-8 predominantly | Weeks 6-12 increasingly |

## Filter by specialty, then mix

Early on, filter questions to the specialty you are revising so that you consolidate one area at a time. But the exam does not arrive in neat blocks; consecutive questions jump from renal physiology to dermatology to a statistics calculation. From about a third of the way through your plan, add a weekly mixed block drawn from every specialty you have covered so far. Mixed practice (interleaving) is harder and feels less productive, but it produces more durable learning and more accurate recall under exam conditions.

## Spaced repetition

Forgetting is predictable: without review, most new facts fade within days. Spaced repetition schedules reviews at expanding intervals, just before you would otherwise forget, so that each review costs little and buys a lot. Apply it in two ways.

First, use the bank's built-in review queue or flagging system. Flag every question you got wrong or guessed, and re-attempt flagged questions after roughly three days, then a week, then a month. Only unflag a question when you have answered it correctly, with confidence, on two spaced occasions.

Second, convert high-density facts into flashcards. Suitable material includes drug adverse effects, antibody associations, cytochrome P450 inducers and inhibitors, inheritance patterns, statistics formulae, opioid conversion ratios and tumour markers. MedAscend's flashcard decks are built from the same topics as the textbook and the question bank, so a card you miss can be traced straight back to the explanation.

## Reviewing incorrect answers properly

The review is where the learning happens, and most candidates rush it. For every incorrect or guessed question, work through four steps:

1. **Classify the error.** Was it a knowledge gap (you did not know the fact), a reasoning error (you knew the facts but combined them wrongly), a reading error (you missed a key word such as "least" or "most likely next step"), or a guess that happened to be wrong? Knowledge gaps need reading; reasoning and reading errors need technique
2. **Read the whole explanation,** including why each distractor is wrong. Then find the topic in the textbook and read the relevant section to place the fact in context
3. **Write one line in your own words** in a running error log organised by specialty. Not the whole explanation; the single fact or principle that would have got you the mark
4. **Flag for spaced re-attempt** as described above

Reviewing correct answers matters too when you were unsure. A right answer reached by a coin toss is a knowledge gap in disguise.

## Use the analytics

Your bank's dashboard shows percentage correct by specialty and how that is changing over time. Check it weekly and compare it against the exam blueprint. A 55 percent score in Clinical Sciences (25 questions in the exam) is a far bigger problem than 55 percent in Medical Ophthalmology (4 questions). Direct your reading time to the specialties where the product of question weight and weakness is greatest. Also watch your timing data: if your average time per question in timed mode drifts above two minutes, you are over-deliberating and need to practise committing.

## Mock exams

A full mock is 200 questions in two three-hour sittings on the same day, mimicking the real timetable including the break. Sit at least two, ideally three, in the final month. Mocks train stamina, reveal how your accuracy decays in the third hour and force you to practise time management, which no amount of 40-question blocks will do. Treat the review of a mock as a two-evening project, not an afterthought, and record your scaled score estimate so that you can see the trajectory.

## What to avoid

- Doing questions passively while watching television; if you are not committing to an answer and reading the explanation, you are wasting the question
- Repeating the same bank from scratch and mistaking recognition of the stem for knowledge
- Ignoring explanations for questions you got right
- Spending more than a few minutes on any single question during review; note it, flag it and move on
- Starting timed mocks too late to act on what they reveal

## Summary

Learn in tutor mode, rehearse in timed mode, mix specialties as you progress, review every wrong answer with a classified error log, and let spaced repetition and the analytics dashboard steer your remaining time. The question bank will teach you the exam if you let it.

title: Exam-Day Strategy: Managing Time in Best-of-Five Papers
excerpt: How to pace two three-hour papers, handle questions you cannot answer, avoid the classic best-of-five traps and arrive at the test centre calm and ready.
author: MedAscend Editorial Team
content:
## The arithmetic of the day

MRCP Part 1 is two papers of 100 best-of-five questions, each lasting three hours, sat on the same day with a break between them. Three hours for 100 questions is 108 seconds per question. In practice you should aim for around 90 seconds per question on the first pass, which leaves roughly 30 minutes at the end of each paper to return to flagged items and check your work. There is no negative marking, so every question must have an answer before time is called, even if that answer is a guess.

## Before the day

- Confirm your test centre booking, address and travel time; visit the location beforehand if it is unfamiliar
- Check the identification requirements: an in-date photographic ID matching the name on your application is essential and you will not be admitted without it
- Plan an early night for the two nights before the exam; the night immediately before is often disturbed by nerves, so bank sleep in advance
- Pack water, a snack for the break, layers of clothing (test centres vary in temperature) and any permitted items listed in your confirmation
- Stop new learning 24 hours before. Read your one-page summaries, then close the books

## Pacing within a paper

Set checkpoints. At one hour you should be at or past question 40; at two hours, past question 80; that leaves the final hour for the last 20 questions and review. On a computer-based exam the on-screen timer and question counter make these checkpoints easy to monitor. If you fall more than five questions behind a checkpoint, speed up by committing faster on questions where you are torn between two options rather than by skimming stems.

Do not let one question steal time from others. If after 90 seconds you have not settled, choose the option you are leaning towards, flag it and move on. Coming back with fresh eyes often resolves the question in seconds, and even if it does not, you have protected the marks available further into the paper.

## Reading the stem

Best-of-five questions reward disciplined reading. Read the final sentence, the actual question, first: "What is the most likely diagnosis?" and "What is the most appropriate next investigation?" demand different processing of the same scenario. Then read the stem once, carefully, noting the age, sex, timeline, key positive findings and numerical results. Look for the discriminating detail the examiner has planted: the travel history, the drug started three weeks ago, the potassium level, the family history.

Beware qualifiers. "Most likely", "most appropriate next step", "least likely", "best initial" and "definitive" each change the correct answer. Candidates lose more marks to misreading these than to genuine knowledge gaps.

## Working the options

- Cover the options and form your own answer from the stem before you look; if your answer is there, it is probably right
- Eliminate options you can rule out with certainty; going from five to two options doubles the value of an educated guess
- When two options remain, return to the stem and ask which detail was included to separate them. Examiners rarely add information without purpose
- Prefer the option that is true for the whole stem rather than one that fits only part of it
- Be wary of options containing absolute words or those that are true statements but do not answer the question asked
- Do not change an answer unless you have identified a specific reason, such as a misread word or a recalled fact. Vague unease is not a reason; first instincts are correct more often than not

## Handling the unknown

Every candidate meets questions that seem to come from nowhere. That is by design: the exam samples the whole of medicine and nobody knows everything. Treat these questions calmly. Use the stem for clues, eliminate what you can, pick the most plausible remaining option, flag it and move on. One unknown question is worth half a percent; the damage comes from letting it rattle you for the next ten.

## The break

Use the break to eat, drink, use the toilet and step outside if possible. Do not discuss paper one with other candidates or check answers; a perceived bad first paper is a common experience and is often wrong, and you cannot change it. Focus on resetting for paper two, where fatigue rather than knowledge becomes the main threat. A short walk and a few minutes of deliberate slow breathing before you sit back down measurably improve concentration in the third hour.

## The final thirty minutes

Return to flagged questions in order. Give each a fresh read and a decision. Then, if time remains, scan for any question left unanswered; on the computer-based interface the review screen shows this clearly. Finally, resist the urge to re-examine questions you answered confidently. Confident answers changed under time pressure are more often changed from right to wrong.

## A checklist for the day

| Stage | Action |
|---|---|
| Night before | Bag packed, ID checked, alarm set, early night |
| Morning | Normal breakfast, arrive 30-45 minutes early |
| Paper start | Read the instructions, note the finish time, set hourly checkpoints |
| During | 90 seconds per question, flag and move on, answer everything |
| Break | Eat, drink, breathe, do not post-mortem paper one |
| Final 30 minutes | Flagged questions first, then confirm nothing is blank |
| After | Leave it behind; results arrive in around six weeks |

## Summary

Pacing, disciplined reading and a refusal to be derailed by unfamiliar questions are worth as many marks as several weeks of revision. Practise them in every timed block and mock so that on the day they are habits rather than intentions. You have prepared for this; let the preparation do the work.
